opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the worst response is despair, and I see a lot of it. People feel that if they can't train a model with thousands of GPUs, they can't do meaningful work anymore. I don't buy that.

First, a lot of the most important science doesn't require frontier scale. Much of what we understand about neural networks came from small experiments that were carefully designed. When I worked on the lottery ticket stuff, most of the insight came from small networks where you could run an experiment many times and actually see what was going on. The questions that matter, like why these models work, what they learn, how training dynamics behave, and what data does, can often be studied at a scale an academic lab can afford. You just have to be disciplined about which findings transfer to scale and which don't.

Second, academics have a comparative advantage that industry often doesn't: time and freedom to be wrong. In industry, and I say this as someone who's spent years building companies, you're under pressure to ship something that works this quarter. Academics can chase the weird question, the thing that might take three years and might not pan out. That's where I'd encourage people to lean in, rather than trying to compete on the same leaderboard with a fraction of the compute. You're going to lose that race, and it's not a race worth running.

Third, evaluation and measurement are wide open and badly needed. We're all building these enormous systems, and frankly we don't know how to tell whether they're good at the things we care about. Benchmarks saturate, contaminate, and don't reflect real use. Figuring out how to measure these models rigorously is deeply intellectual work, it's undervalued, and it doesn't need a giant cluster.

And finally, efficiency. If compute is the bottleneck, then making things cheaper is both a research agenda and a democratizing force. A lot of what we did at Mosaic came from the belief that if you can bring the cost of training down by a large factor, you change who gets to participate. That's a great problem for academics, because every improvement compounds for everyone.

So I'd say: don't try to be a small OpenAI. Be a scientist. Ask the questions the big labs don't have the patience or incentive to ask, and be rigorous about it. That's always been academia's role, and I don't think foundation models change that. If anything, they make it more important.

r001.rationale: The response does not compare the current focus on foundation models with the field’s narrowing from machine learning to deep learning in 2017–2018.

r002.rationale: The response argues that smaller-scale and other research can be meaningful and useful, including foundational science, evaluation, and efficiency.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot, because I lived through that transition. I was a PhD student at MIT when the lottery ticket work happened, and the whole premise of that line of research was that you could poke at a ResNet on a single GPU and learn something fundamental. And then somewhere around 2020, it started to feel like the center of gravity moved to places where you needed thousands of accelerators just to ask the interesting question.

My honest answer is that I don't think academics should try to compete on the thing industry is best at, which is scale. You're not going to out-train OpenAI or Google or, frankly, Databricks from a university lab. That's a losing game and it's demoralizing to play it. But I also really push back on the idea that this means academia is irrelevant now. I think it's the opposite.

There are a few things universities are uniquely positioned to do. One is the science. Industry labs are under enormous pressure to ship. We do a lot of empirical work, but we often don't have time to understand why something works. Why do scaling laws look the way they do? What's actually going on with emergence, or is it an artifact of how we measure things? Those are questions you can attack with careful, small-scale experiments if you're clever about it, and the answers matter at every scale. Some of the most influential papers of the last few years were not the biggest ones.

The second thing is that academia can afford to be contrarian. When everybody in industry has converged on one recipe, the university is where someone should be asking whether that recipe is wrong. If everyone is doing transformers, somebody should be seriously trying alternatives, not because it's guaranteed to pay off, but because the expected value of a few people doing that is enormous and nobody else has the incentive.

And third, I'd say evaluation, data, and the stuff around the model. Benchmarks, understanding what's in the training data, figuring out what these systems can and can't do. That work is undervalued inside companies and critically important, and it doesn't require a giant cluster.

The thing I'd caution against is the mindset of "I'll just fine-tune a model someone else released and call it a day." That's fine as a tool, but if your whole research agenda depends on what a company decides to open-source next quarter, you've given up your independence. So pick problems where the scale isn't the point.

And then the practical piece: I do think we need more shared compute for academics, and I think industry has a responsibility there. Open models, open datasets, open training logs where possible. That's part of why I cared so much about doing things like MPT in the open. The more of the pipeline that's visible, the more academics can actually do science on it rather than guessing.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift toward large-scale work around 2020, but does not compare it to machine learning’s narrowing toward deep learning in 2017–2018.

r002.rationale: The response does not say non-large-model research is unlikely to matter; it argues that small-scale science, contrarian research, and evaluation remain valuable.

astra-6.text:
I think the first thing is to resist the idea that academic research has to look like industry research, just with a smaller budget. If you frame the problem as, “How do I train a bigger model than a company that has vastly more compute than I do?” you’ve picked a pretty difficult game to win. But training the biggest model isn’t the only interesting scientific question.

There’s an enormous amount we don’t understand about these systems. What actually matters in the data? How do you evaluate whether a model is doing what you think it’s doing? Can you get the same capabilities with much less computation? Those are questions where a careful experiment and a good idea can still be incredibly valuable.

And academia has a different incentive structure. You can challenge an assumption that everybody in industry is building on. You can spend time understanding why something fails, even if that doesn’t immediately lead to a product. I’d like to see us take advantage of that freedom.

That doesn’t mean access to compute isn’t a real problem. It is, and we should work to improve access. But I wouldn’t want academic researchers to conclude that they’re irrelevant because they can’t train the largest model. There’s a lot of room to decide which questions deserve to be asked in the first place.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing is to resist the idea that, if you can’t train the biggest model, you can’t do meaningful research. If the goal is to compete with an industrial lab on scale, that’s a pretty difficult position for a university to be in. But that’s not the only way to contribute.

Academia has an opportunity to step back and ask questions that aren’t necessarily aligned with shipping the next product. Why do these models work? What actually matters in training them? Can we make them cheaper to train and use? How do we study their limitations in a way that produces reliable scientific knowledge?

At the same time, we have to be careful about what our experiments establish. If you study something on a small model, that can be valuable, but whether it carries over to a much larger model is a question you have to test, not an assumption you get for free.

So I’d like to see both more access to computational resources for academics and more creativity about the questions we ask. Universities shouldn’t have to become smaller versions of industrial labs to have an important role in the field.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the shift toward large foundation models but does not compare it to the field’s narrowing from machine learning to deep learning around 2017–2018.

r002.rationale: The response argues that research beyond competing to train the largest models can still contribute meaningfully, rather than saying unrelated research is unlikely to be interesting or useful.
